result: Forskolin-induced HSV-1 reactivation requires neuronal excitation mediated by ion channel activity. Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels (TTX), voltage-gated potassium channels (TEA), or HCN channels (ZD 7288, Ivabradine, CsCl) significantly reduced forskolin-mediated reactivation and Phase I viral gene expression, and blocked hyperexcitability-associated histone modifications.
evaluation: Claims C2, C50, C62, C110-C116 collectively demonstrate that forskolin-induced reactivation depends on neuronal excitation through ion channel activity. Multiple independent pharmacological inhibitors targeting different ion channels (TTX, TEA, ZD 7288, Ivabradine, CsCl) consistently blocked reactivation, Phase I gene expression, and histone modifications (Figures 4A-F). The convergence of evidence from multiple inhibitors and readouts (GFP-positive neurons, viral mRNA, histone modifications) strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Direct induction of neuronal hyperexcitability triggers HSV-1 reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner. KCl treatment and TTX-release, which directly induce hyperexcitability, triggered reactivation that was blocked by DLK and JNK inhibitors. Chronic hyperexcitability (≥8 hours) was required for robust reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C3, C51, C117-C122 demonstrate that direct hyperexcitability induction triggers reactivation. KCl treatment and TTX-release (which induces synaptic scaling and hyperexcitability) both triggered reactivation (Figures 5A-B), and this was blocked by DLK/JNK inhibitors and DLK knockdown (Figures 5B-C). The requirement for prolonged treatment (≥8 hours) supports chronic hyperexcitability as the trigger. The convergence of pharmacological and genetic evidence strongly supports this result.

result: Forskolin-induced reactivation is dependent on DLK/JNK activation. Both pharmacological inhibition (SP600125 for JNK, GNE-3511 for DLK) and shRNA-mediated DLK knockdown blocked forskolin-mediated reactivation and Phase I viral gene expression at 20 hours post-stimulus.
evaluation: Claims C4, C52, C72-C73, C81-C84 demonstrate DLK/JNK dependence through multiple approaches. Pharmacological inhibitors (SP600125, GNE-3511) blocked both full reactivation (Figures 2A-B) and Phase I gene expression (Figures 2G-I). shRNA-mediated DLK knockdown (>90-fold reduction, Figure 2J) also blocked reactivation and Phase I gene expression (Figures 2K-L). The convergence of pharmacological and genetic evidence with multiple readouts strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Forskolin-induced reactivation includes a Phase I wave of viral gene expression that is independent of histone demethylase activity. Viral lytic gene expression (including late genes) occurred at 20 hours before DNA replication (48 hours), and was not blocked by LSD1 inhibitors (OG-L002, S 2101) or UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor (GSK-J4), though these inhibitors blocked full reactivation at 72 hours.
evaluation: Claims C5, C54, C80, C90, C103-C109 demonstrate Phase I independence from histone demethylases. Viral gene expression (ICP27, ICP4, ICP8, UL30, UL48, gC) was significantly upregulated at 20 hours (Figures 2D-F), before DNA replication at 48 hours (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). LSD1 and UTX/JMJD3 inhibitors blocked full reactivation (Figures 3—figure supplement 1F-G) but not Phase I gene expression at 20 hours (Figures 3C-F). This temporal and pharmacological dissociation strongly supports Phase I independence from histone demethylases.

result: Forskolin-induced reactivation is linked to a histone methyl/phospho switch on viral genomes. Forskolin treatment induced transient H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hours that returned to baseline by 10 hours. Viral genomes co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p at significantly higher levels at 5 and 20 hours post-forskolin treatment compared to mock.
evaluation: Claims C6, C99-C102, C140 demonstrate histone methyl/phospho switch involvement. Forskolin induced transient H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hours (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B). Click-chemistry visualization showed viral genomes significantly co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p at 5 and 20 hours (Figures 3A-B). Combined with Phase I independence from histone demethylases (C105, C109), this supports the methyl/phospho switch mechanism. However, the functional requirement for this modification was not directly tested (e.g., with kinase inhibitors), which would strengthen the conclusion.

result: IL-1β triggers HSV-1 reactivation in mature sympathetic neurons via neuronal excitability and DLK activation. IL-1β treatment induced reactivation that was blocked by IL-1R antibody, TTX (voltage-gated sodium channel inhibitor), DLK inhibitor (GNE-3511), and DLK knockdown.
evaluation: Claims C11, C61, C131-C137 demonstrate IL-1β-induced reactivation through multiple lines of evidence. IL-1β triggered reactivation in mature neurons (Figure 7A), which was blocked by IL-1R antibody (Figure 7B), TTX (Figure 7C), DLK inhibitor (Figure 7C), and DLK knockdown (Figure 7D). The convergence of receptor-specific, ion channel, and DLK-targeting approaches strongly supports this conclusion. However, variability in reactivation levels was noted, likely reflecting neuronal heterogeneity.

result: IL-1β induces neuronal hyperexcitability in mature sympathetic neurons. IL-1β treatment induced hyperexcitability-associated markers (γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p) and increased cytosolic Ca2+ responses to acetylcholine. These effects were blocked by TTX and IL-1R antibody.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C123, C125-C130, C141-C142 demonstrate IL-1β-induced hyperexcitability through multiple readouts. IL-1β induced γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p in mature neurons (Figures 6A-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), which were blocked by TTX and IL-1R antibody (Figures 6B-C). IL-1β also increased Ca2+ responses to acetylcholine (Figures 6D-F), blocked by IL-1R antibody (Figure 6F). The convergence of histone modification and functional Ca2+ imaging data strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Forskolin-induced reactivation requires activation of adenylate cyclase and increased intracellular cAMP. Forskolin, but not cell-impermeable dd-forskolin, triggered robust reactivation. The cAMP mimetic 8-bromo-cAMP was sufficient to trigger reactivation, and adenylate cyclase inhibitor SQ22,536 significantly diminished reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 demonstrate cAMP requirement through multiple approaches. Forskolin triggered robust reactivation while dd-forskolin did not (Figure 1C), though dd-forskolin showed marginal activity (p=0.07 by ANOVA, p=0.03 by t-test). The cAMP mimetic 8-bromo-cAMP triggered reactivation (Figure 1D), and adenylate cyclase inhibitor SQ22,536 blocked reactivation (Figure 1E). The convergence of evidence supports cAMP requirement, though the marginal dd-forskolin activity suggests possible minor extracellular effects.

result: Forskolin-induced Phase I reactivation does not depend on PKA, CREB, EPAC1, or EPAC2. PKA inhibitor (KT 5720), CREB inhibitor (666-15), and EPAC1 inhibitor (ESI09) did not block Phase I gene expression at 20 hours, though PKA and CREB inhibitors blocked full reactivation at 3 days. EPAC2 inhibitor (SQ22,536) did not block 8-bromo-cAMP-induced reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C85-C90 demonstrate Phase I independence from canonical cAMP effectors through pharmacological inhibition. PKA inhibitor blocked full reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but not Phase I (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). CREB inhibitor showed similar pattern (Figures 2—figure supplement 2C-D). EPAC1 inhibitor did not block reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), and EPAC2 inhibitor did not block 8-bromo-cAMP-induced reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F). The convergence of negative results with multiple inhibitors supports this conclusion, though genetic validation would strengthen it.

result: Forskolin-induced reactivation exhibits slower kinetics and affects a subpopulation of latently-infected neurons compared to superinfection. Us11-GFP synthesis appeared at 48 hours and peaked at 72 hours post-forskolin, while superinfection induced GFP by 24 hours. Forskolin triggered reactivation in approximately 1 in 3.4 neurons compared to superinfection. Viral DNA replication was not detected until 48 hours.
evaluation: Claims C74-C79 characterize forskolin-induced reactivation kinetics through multiple readouts. Us11-GFP synthesis was delayed (48-72 hours) compared to superinfection (24 hours) (Figure 2C). Viral DNA replication occurred at 48-72 hours (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). Viral mRNA (ICP27, ICP4, ICP8, UL30, UL48, gC) was upregulated at 20 hours (Figures 2D-F). The comparison to superinfection provides important context, though the subpopulation calculation (1 in 3.4) assumes all neurons are equally infected, which may not be accurate.

result: Forskolin treatment induces markers of neuronal hyperexcitability (γH2AX, cFOS) without loss of AKT phosphorylation, indicating a mechanism distinct from PI3K/AKT inhibition. Forskolin induced γH2AX at 5 hours (resolved by 15 hours) and increased cFOS at 5 hours. Both forskolin and PI3K inhibitor activated JNK (increased c-Jun phosphorylation), but only PI3K inhibitor reduced pAKT.
evaluation: Claims C91-C98 demonstrate forskolin induces hyperexcitability markers without AKT dephosphorylation. Forskolin induced transient γH2AX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C) and cFOS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) at 5 hours. Forskolin did not reduce pAKT at 15 hours, while PI3K inhibitor did (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). Both activated JNK (increased c-Jun phosphorylation). This temporal and mechanistic dissociation from PI3K/AKT pathway is well-supported and distinguishes forskolin-induced reactivation from NGF deprivation.

result: IL-1β did not induce the same changes in γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p in post-natal neurons as in mature neurons.
evaluation: Claim C124 states an observation but provides no data or quantification. The manuscript mentions this difference but does not show data for post-natal neurons, making it impossible to evaluate the extent or significance of this difference. This observation requires additional data to be properly evaluated.

result: Background and context claims about HSV-1 biology, latency, reactivation mechanisms, DLK/JNK signaling, histone modifications, and IL-1β from prior literature.
evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C49, C56-C60 represent established knowledge and prior literature cited in the introduction and discussion. These claims are appropriately cited and represent accurate summaries of prior work. They provide essential context for the current study but are not novel findings from this manuscript.

result: HSV-1 co-opts neuronal hyperexcitability and IL-1β signaling to induce reactivation via DLK/JNK activation. IL-1β is released under stress, fever, and UV exposure (known HSV reactivation triggers), and the study identifies IL-1β as a novel physiological trigger acting via neuronal hyperexcitability with DLK/JNK signaling central to reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C14, C64-C65, C138-C139, C143-C144 represent the major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. The link between IL-1β release conditions (stress, fever, UV) and known HSV triggers is well-established (C7-C8). The experimental data strongly support IL-1β as a novel trigger acting via hyperexcitability and DLK (C11-C13, C61-C63, C131-C137). The central role of DLK/JNK is supported across multiple stimuli (forskolin, KCl, TTX-release, IL-1β). These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent experimental evidence, though in vivo validation would strengthen them.
